headline: TikTok users skip showers to attract partners

sources.title: Forbes: 'Pheromone Maxxing' TikTok Dating Trend Has People Not Showering
Vice: Introducing Pheromone Maxxing, TikTok's Latest Disgusting Dating Trend
MedBound Times: Teen Trend 'Pheromone Maxxing': Social Media & Health Risks Explained

chunks.text: A TikTok trend called "pheromone maxxing" has {{caught on}} this month. Forbes reported on it on August 16, and other [[news outlets]] followed. Followers {{give up}} daily showers and {{go without}} [[deodorant]]. A few even drink [[urine]]. They believe soap and water {{wash off}} a natural "musk" of sex pheromones that attracts [[potential partners]]. The trend {{grew out of}} "looksmaxxing," an older TikTok trend about improving your [[appearance]].

verbs.wrong: To reach the same level as others
verbs.why: A new dance can catch on in a single weekend, and a slang word can catch on across a whole school. The pheromone maxxing trend caught on this month after Forbes first reported on it on August 16.

verbs.wrong: To release a smell into the air
verbs.why: Some people give up sugar for a month, and a runner may give up racing after an injury. People who follow this trend give up daily showers in the hope of smelling more attractive.

verbs.correct: To not use something you normally use
verbs.wrong: To agree with what other people do
verbs.why: A camper can go without hot water for a week, and a busy worker may go without lunch on a hard day. Followers of the trend go without deodorant because they think it hides a natural body musk.

verbs.wrong: To slowly lose its effect over time
verbs.why: Rain washes off the mud on a car, and a quick rinse washes off the soap in your hair. Trend followers believe soap and water wash off a natural musk that contains sex pheromones.

verbs.wrong: To change from a child into an adult
verbs.why: A big company can grow out of a small college project, and many festivals grow out of local traditions. Pheromone maxxing grew out of looksmaxxing, an older TikTok trend about looking as attractive as possible.

chunks.text: The science does not {{hold up}}: in over 60 years of research, no human sex pheromone has been confirmed. A 2025 review called one chemical in male [[sweat]] "[[inconclusive]]." Experts {{point out}} that the organ other [[mammals]] use to detect pheromones is small and underdeveloped in humans. People also {{mix up}} the trend with the "sweaty T-shirt" studies, which found women prefer the [[body odor]] of men with different immune genes. That preference is real, but it does not attract partners, and hormonal [[birth control]] [[reverses]] it.

verbs.why: A weak excuse does not hold up when a parent asks questions, and a good theory holds up in experiment after experiment. Researchers say the science behind this trend does not hold up, since no human sex pheromone has ever been confirmed.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To measure something in a study
verbs.why: A teacher points out mistakes in an essay, and a friend points out that the deadline is tomorrow. Experts point out that the organ animals use to detect pheromones is small and probably underdeveloped in humans.

verbs.wrong: To invent a story that is not true
verbs.why: People mix up the names of twins, and travelers mix up two cities with similar names. Part of the problem is that people mix up the trend with real research, like the sweaty T-shirt studies.

chunks.text: Doctors warn of real health risks. When people stop washing, bacteria and sweat {{build up}} on the skin, and some {{come down with}} [[skin infections]], including fungal ones, or respiratory infections. Others buy [[unregulated]] "pheromone" oils and sprays and {{end up}} with [[allergic reactions]]. Drinking urine is worse: it contains [[waste products]] and harmful microbes. No evidence shows that avoiding [[hygiene]] increases pheromone effects. Feeling more attractive, experts say, is a [[boost]] in confidence, not body chemistry.

verbs.correct: To slowly collect in one place
verbs.wrong: To suddenly appear on the skin
verbs.why: Dust builds up on shelves nobody cleans, and ice builds up on a plane's wings in cold weather. When people stop washing, bacteria and sweat build up on the skin and can lead to infections.

verbs.correct: To become sick with an illness
verbs.wrong: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.why: Half a class can come down with the flu in winter, and travelers often come down with a cold after a long flight. Some people who stop washing come down with skin infections, including fungal infections.

verbs.correct: To reach a result you did not plan
verbs.why: A lost driver can end up in the wrong town, and a tired cook can end up ordering pizza again. A few people who buy unregulated pheromone sprays end up with allergic reactions.

chunks.text: Many followers are teenagers, and researchers are not surprised. [[Adolescents]] are still {{figuring out}} who they are, and friends strongly influence them. A 2025 study on [[viral challenges]] described "[[social proof]]": when many people online seem to be doing something, it looks normal and safe. Teens then {{take up}} a challenge quickly and often {{buy into}} the idea behind it. Doctors' advice is simple: skipping showers will not help anyone find a partner. Hygiene still matters.

verbs.wrong: To exercise to keep the body fit
verbs.why: It can take an hour to figure out a paper map, and students spend years figuring out what to study. Researchers say adolescents are still figuring out who they are, so friends have a strong influence on what they do.

verbs.wrong: To look or act like a parent
verbs.why: A retired father might take up painting, and more kids take up chess every year. When something looks normal and safe online, teens take up a challenge quickly.

verbs.wrong: To bring a good result later
verbs.why: Not everyone buys into the idea that money brings happiness, and many fans buy into rumors about their favorite band. Thanks to social proof, teens often buy into the idea behind a challenge.

mainIdea.s: A viral TikTok trend tells people to skip showers so their natural scent will attract dates. Scientists say no human sex pheromone has been proven, and doctors warn the habit brings infections.
mainIdea.why: No human sex pheromone has been confirmed in more than 60 years of research, and doctors link the habit to skin, fungal, and respiratory infections.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that skipping showers really makes people smell more attractive, because sweat carries immune signals. Doctors still warn against the trend, since unwashed skin can cause infections.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the science does not hold up. The sweaty T-shirt studies show a real preference, not a scent that attracts partners, and any benefit is likely psychological.

mainIdea.s: A TikTok skincare trend has teenagers buying strong anti-aging creams made for adults. Dermatologists report more young patients with rashes and damaged skin, and some brands now add age warnings.
mainIdea.why: The trend is about skipping showers and deodorant to keep a natural scent. There are no anti-aging creams, dermatologists, or age warnings here.

tf.s: People mix up the trend with real body-odor research.

tf.s: Pheromone maxxing grew out of the sweaty T-shirt studies.
tf.why: The trend grew out of looksmaxxing, an older TikTok trend about improving your appearance. The sweaty T-shirt studies are separate research that people mix up with the trend.

tf.why: When many people online seem to be doing something, it looks normal and safe, and teens often buy into the idea behind it.

lines.text: Did you see this pheromone maxxing thing? People are {{giving up}} showers to smell more attractive.
[[You can't make this stuff up]]. On purpose?
On purpose. They {{go without}} deodorant too, because they think soap {{washes off}} some natural musk that attracts partners.
And that actually {{caught on}}? Does the science {{hold up}} at all?
Not really. Researchers {{point out}} that nobody has confirmed a human sex pheromone in 60 years of studies.
So the whole idea [[doesn't pass the smell test]]. Where did it even come from?
It {{grew out of}} looksmaxxing. And people {{mix it up}} with those sweaty T-shirt studies, which were about something different.
Using a T-shirt study to justify skipping showers is [[a stretch]]. And doesn't all that sweat just {{build up}}?
It does. Some people {{come down with}} skin infections, and others {{end up}} with allergic reactions from cheap sprays.
So you could ruin your skin and still not find a date.
That's what doctors say. If you feel more attractive after a week without soap, it's [[all in your head]], not your body chemistry.
[[Count me out]], then. I'm not {{buying into}} any of it, and I'm keeping my shower.
Neither am I. Though I get why teens {{take it up}}. They're still {{figuring out}} who they are, and friends have a big influence.
[[Monkey see, monkey do]]. When everyone online is doing something, it starts to look normal.
